drills.title: Integer division into a double
drills.promptMd: What does this program print? Commit to an answer before reasoning through it.
drills.explanationMd: Both operands of `/` are `int`, so C++ performs integer division first — `3 / 4` is `0` with the fraction discarded — and only *then* widens that `0` to `0.0` for storage in `result`. The type of the destination variable has no effect on how the division is computed; to get `0.75`, you must cast at least one operand *before* dividing: `static_cast<double>(numerator) / denominator`.

drills.title: Remainder and negative numbers
drills.promptMd: Both `a` and `b` test whether `x` is odd. What does this print?
drills.explanationMd: In C++, the result of `%` takes the sign of the *left* operand, so `-7 % 2` is `-1`, not `1`. Therefore `a` (`-1 == 1`) is `false` (prints `0`), while `b` (`-1 != 0`) is `true` (prints `1`). The safe idiom for an oddness test is always `!= 0`; the `== 1` form silently fails for any negative odd number.

drills.title: Prefix vs postfix: what value is captured?
drills.promptMd: Trace `x` carefully through both increments. What does this print?
drills.explanationMd: `x++` (postfix) copies the *old* value of `x` (10) into `a` and then increments `x` to 11. `++x` (prefix) increments `x` to 12 first and then copies the *new* value (12) into `b`. The key distinction: postfix yields the value before the change; prefix yields the value after. After both lines, `x` itself is 12.

drills.title: Fix the oddness test for negative numbers
drills.promptMd: The function returns wrong results for negative odd numbers. Fix it so all tests pass.
drills.explanationMd: C++'s `%` gives a result with the sign of the left operand, so `-7 % 2` is `-1` — which is not `== 1`, causing `isOdd(-7)` to return `false`. Replacing `== 1` with `!= 0` fixes this: any non-zero remainder, whether `1` or `-1`, correctly signals an odd number.

drills.title: Fix floating-point equality
drills.promptMd: The function ignores its `epsilon` parameter entirely. Fix it so `0.1 + 0.2` compares equal to `0.3` within the given tolerance.
drills.explanationMd: Because most decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary, `0.1 + 0.2` and `0.3` differ by a tiny rounding error — so `== 0.0` returns `false` even when they are conceptually equal. The fix is to compare the *magnitude* of the difference (`std::abs(a - b)`) against the tolerance `epsilon` using `<=`; using `<=` instead of `<` also allows an `epsilon` of `0` to still report truly identical values as equal.

drills.title: Write clampedPercentage
drills.promptMd: Implement `clampedPercentage(covered, total)`: return coverage as a percentage in `[0.0, 100.0]`, or `0.0` when `total <= 0`. Watch out for integer division.
drills.explanationMd: The guard `if (total <= 0) return 0.0;` prevents division by zero and handles a degenerate total. The cast `static_cast<double>(covered)` promotes the numerator to `double` *before* the division, so C++ performs floating-point division and preserves the fraction; without the cast, `1 / 3` would be `0` via integer division and the result would always be a whole-number percentage.
